title: Mass vs. Weight
hook: Your mass is the same on the Moon as on Earth — but your weight isn't. They're related, but they are not the same thing.
key_points: Mass measures how much matter an object contains and how hard it is to accelerate.
Weight is the force of gravity pulling on that mass: weight = mass times gravity.
Mass stays constant everywhere; weight changes with the local gravity.
A scale reads weight, but kilograms label mass — which is why the numbers can confuse.
content_html: Everyday language treats mass and weight as the same, but physics keeps them apart. Mass is a measure of how much matter is in an object — and equivalently how hard it is to accelerate it, the m in F = ma. Weight is something different: it's the force gravity exerts on that mass, found by multiplying mass by the local gravitational pull.
extra_html: Because mass is intrinsic to the object, it doesn't change when you travel. Weight does: take the same person to the Moon, where gravity is about a sixth of Earth's, and they weigh about a sixth as much while their mass is unchanged. A bathroom scale actually measures weight (a force), even though it's labeled in kilograms, a unit of mass — which is exactly why the two ideas get tangled. Britannica lays out the distinction and the units involved.

related.title: Newton's Three Laws of Motion
related.hook: Three short rules — inertia, F=ma, and action-reaction — quietly govern almost everything that moves around you.

flashcards.prompt: Why does your weight change on the Moon but your mass does not?
flashcards.back_html: Mass is the amount of matter you contain and never changes. Weight is the pull of gravity on that mass, and the Moon's gravity is weaker.

flashcards.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes mass from weight?

choices.text: Mass measures amount of matter; weight is the force of gravity on it
Weight measures amount of matter; mass is the force of gravity on it
Mass and weight are two words for the exact same quantity

flashcards.explanation_html: Mass is intrinsic to the object; weight depends on the local gravity acting on that mass.
